summary: Psalm 143 is a plea from a servant who asks Yahweh to hear him without entering into judgment against him. The speaker describes being pursued and crushed, then turns to memory, thirst, trust, and repeated requests for rescue, guidance, revival, and judgment against enemies.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows lament as direct speech to God: distress, confession of human unrighteousness, remembrance, and desire for guidance are held together. It belongs in Book V of Psalms, where prayers of trouble continue inside the collection’s larger movement toward praise.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David.” In Psalms, Davidic headings are ancient features of the received collection, but readers differ on whether each one marks authorship, association, dedication, collection, or reception.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the psalms for prayer and worship.
context.date: The anthology may preserve poems from the monarchy through the postexilic period; this prayer names no specific historical occasion that would securely date it.
context.setting: The poem speaks from an unnamed crisis involving enemies, inner collapse, and fear of deathlike abandonment. Its precise original occasion is not given in the chapter.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer, specifically an individual lament with petition, complaint, memory, trust, and appeal for guidance.

outline.heading: A Plea To Be Heard
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to hear his prayer and immediately appeals for mercy, since no living person is righteous before God’s judgment.

outline.heading: The Enemy And The Inner Collapse
outline.note: The threat is described as pursuit, being struck down, darkness, and a desolate heart.

outline.heading: Memory And Thirst
outline.note: The speaker remembers God’s past works, stretches out his hands, and compares his need for God to parched land.

outline.heading: Urgent Requests For Nearness And Direction
outline.note: The prayer asks for a quick answer, for God not to hide his face, and for morning loving kindness and the way to walk.

outline.heading: Rescue And Instruction
outline.note: The speaker flees to Yahweh for shelter and asks to be taught God’s will and led in uprightness.

outline.heading: Revival And Judgment
outline.note: The psalm closes by asking Yahweh to revive and rescue the speaker and to cut off those who afflict him.

keyVerses.text: Don’t enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no man living is righteous.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm’s humility: the speaker asks for help while acknowledging that no living person can claim righteousness before God.

keyVerses.text: I spread out my hands to you. My soul thirsts for you, like a parched land. Selah.
keyVerses.why: The image gathers the chapter’s longing into one picture: the speaker needs God as dry ground needs water.

keyVerses.text: Cause me to hear your loving kindness in the morning, for I trust in you. Cause me to know the way in which I should walk, for I lift up my soul to you.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns the lament toward guidance, asking not only for relief from danger but for a path to walk.

keyVerses.text: Teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your Spirit is good. Lead me in the land of uprightness.
keyVerses.why: The chapter’s request for rescue becomes a request for formation: the speaker wants to be taught, led, and aligned with God’s will.

themes: Guidance in the way to walk

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading identifies it as “A Psalm by David.” In Psalms, that heading is important evidence within the received collection, but readers differ on whether such headings always mean direct authorship or sometimes association, dedication, or collection. The chapter itself presents an “I” who prays as Yahweh’s servant under attack.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask God not to enter into judgment?
questions.answer: The speaker appeals to Yahweh’s faithfulness and righteousness for relief, but he also recognizes that judgment would expose human unrighteousness. Verse 2 does not deny the speaker’s need for rescue; it says that the plea rests on mercy rather than on a claim of personal innocence before God.

questions.question: What does “my soul” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In this translation, “my soul” names the speaker’s needy life or self before God. The enemies pursue his soul, his soul thirsts for God, and he asks God to bring his soul out of trouble. The phrase should be read as the speaker’s whole endangered life in prayer, not as a detached object being discussed abstractly.

questions.question: What is the force of the darkness and pit language?
questions.answer: The speaker says the enemy has made him live “in dark places” and fears becoming like those who go down into “the pit.” The chapter uses these images to describe danger, despair, and nearness to death. It does not give a map of the afterlife; it gives the language of a person who feels close to being swallowed by deathlike trouble.

questions.question: Why does remembering the past matter here?
questions.answer: After describing his distress, the speaker says he remembers “the days of old” and meditates on God’s doings. The memory does not instantly remove the trouble, but it changes the direction of the prayer: the speaker turns from the enemy’s pressure to God’s work and reaches out to God in thirst.

questions.question: What does the request for morning loving kindness suggest?
questions.answer: The speaker asks to hear Yahweh’s loving kindness “in the morning” because he trusts in God. The request expresses hope for renewed assurance and direction. The verse joins trust with guidance: the speaker wants to know “the way” he should walk.

questions.question: Is this psalm only asking for rescue, or also for moral direction?
questions.answer: It asks for both. The speaker asks Yahweh to deliver him from enemies, but also says, “Teach me to do your will.” Rescue from danger and instruction in uprightness belong together in the chapter’s final movement.

questions.question: Why does the final verse ask God to cut off and destroy enemies?
questions.answer: Verse 12 is an imprecatory request, asking God to act against those who afflict the speaker’s soul. Readers differ on how such prayers should be used later: some emphasize that the sufferer hands judgment to God rather than taking revenge, while others stress the moral danger of turning these words into personal hostility. The chapter presents the request as part of an ancient lament under threat, not as a simple permission for private vengeance.

questions.question: What role does God’s “Spirit” play in this psalm?
questions.answer: The speaker says, “Your Spirit is good,” while asking to be taught and led. Within the chapter, that means God’s own guidance is the source of the path the speaker needs. The verse does not explain a later doctrine in detail; it uses prayer language for God’s good leading.

glossary.def: A preserved performance marker in some psalms. Its exact ancient function is uncertain, so many translations leave the word in place.
This translation’s phrase for God’s loyal mercy or steadfast care, requested in the morning and appealed to again in the final verse.
A deathlike place or image of going down, used here for what the speaker fears if God hides his face.
The speaker’s self-description before Yahweh. It appears in the plea against judgment and again in the closing appeal.
